title: Listening to babies changes decisions, not just data
excerpt: What we're learning from applying the Mosaic approach in local authority co-design work — and why it changes what gets prioritised, not just what gets recorded.
coverAlt: A toddler's hand reaching for a wooden toy train
body: Most local authority engagement work is built to hear from parents and carers. Far less of it is built to hear from babies and very young children themselves — not because anyone doubts it matters, but because the methods for doing it well aren't widely embedded in day-to-day commissioning and service design.

Over the past year we've been supporting local teams to apply the principles of the Mosaic approach — combining observation, sensory engagement and creative methods — alongside more familiar consultation with families and practitioners. The aim isn't to replace what services already know from parents; it's to check it against what children's own behaviour and responses are actually telling us.

The pattern that keeps showing up is small but consistent: when babies and young children's perspectives are gathered directly, priorities shift. Not dramatically, and not always in ways anyone could have predicted from the adult consultation alone — but enough to change which of several reasonable options a service designs around.

That's the case for treating this as evidence, not sentiment. Evidence that reducing inequalities in the early years means building the infrastructure to listen to the people those systems are ultimately for, at every level of decision-making — not just the level where they can speak for themselves.
